AgentDelta: cross-suite evaluation report

A reproducible, objective-first benchmark for frontier coding agents. This report consolidates every suite run to date into one view: results first, then the full apparatus behind them.

Headline finding

Across 11 suites spanning every difficulty tier we have built, from easy fixes and harder multi-step work to frontier tasks, hard H2 to H5 tasks (multi-tenant authorization, state machines, multi-file root-cause), and a real widened-window concurrency race, all 12 1M-context Claude models verified 95.7% of valid runs. 3 of 36 pairwise model comparisons cleared the materiality bar (success delta above threshold and a significant Holm-corrected paired McNemar test). At single-repository scale, capability is not differentiable among these models.

Where the models do separate is efficiency. Cheapest per run: gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07 ($0.014/run). Fastest per run: gpt-5.4 (1.1m/run).

This is an honest negative result on capability and a positive result on efficiency. It does not say newer models are equivalent in general; it says these tasks do not separate them. See Interpretation for what that means and where a gap is likely to appear.

The separator is efficiency, not capability

Interpretation: what this does and does not mean

What the data supports

  • On objective, hidden-test-graded tasks at single-repository scale, these four 1M-context models are capability-equivalent: none has a material, statistically supported success advantage over the oldest baseline.
  • The benchmark refuses to manufacture a gap: the materiality gate (delta threshold + Holm-corrected McNemar) correctly reports "no difference" rather than promoting noise to a finding.
  • The real, consistent separator is efficiency: cost and latency per verified task, which is exactly the axis a buyer optimizes once correctness is saturated.

What it does not claim

  • It does not claim newer models are pointless. It claims these tasks do not discriminate them. The plausible discriminators, namely multi-service changes, large ambiguous specs, and long-horizon planning across the full 1M context, are not yet in the suite.
  • Saturation is itself the signal: when a tier hits 100% for everyone, the next version must raise difficulty along the dimension that actually taxes a frontier model (scope and ambiguity, not just algorithmic trickiness).
  • The efficiency ranking is real but workload-specific; it should be re-measured per task family.

Per-model comparison

Every metric is a mean over that model's valid runs across all suites. Work signals (tokens, tools, reads, edits) are the basis of the agentic-amplification analysis: a newer model that wins only by doing more work is amplified, not intrinsically better.

Statistical assessment

A gain is promoted to "material" only if it clears both gates: a success improvement of at least the configured threshold (in percentage points) and a significant paired McNemar test after Holm correction across the comparison family. Material gains are then escalated to the Level 2 amplification analysis. This is where the benchmark earns the right to say "no difference."

Methodology

AgentDelta evaluates a model-plus-agent system, not a model in isolation. Every run is a real coding agent (Claude Code or Codex CLI, via inspect_swe) acting inside a pinned Docker sandbox on a seeded git repository, graded by tests the agent never sees. The agent is chosen per run with --agent; the full tech stack is under Stack & requirements.

Execution

  • Harness: Inspect AI drives the task; inspect_swe runs the selected agent CLI (Claude Code or Codex CLI) inside a per-fixture Docker image. The model edits files; nothing else is scripted.
  • Sandbox: one image per fixture, pinned by digest. Network is disabled by default and only enabled for real model runs that need Anthropic API or OpenAI API access.
  • Reasoning effort is a recorded, controllable dimension (low to max) so the same model can be compared across effort settings.
  • Repetitions per (task, model) with blocked randomization of run order, so provider-side variance and ordering effects do not bias one model.

Scoring (objective-first)

A run is verified only if the public tests pass, the pre-existing suite still passes (no regression), and no hard scope or forbidden-shortcut violation occurred. Hidden tests measure how completely the fix generalizes; scope control measures edit discipline. The objective score combines verified success, hidden-test score, regression avoidance, scope control, and set-relative cost/time efficiency.

  • Hard scope violation (touching a forbidden file, or matching a forbidden pattern such as deleting/skipping tests) fails the run.
  • Soft over-budget (too many files or lines) lowers the scope-control component but does not by itself fail a correct fix.
  • Test-writing tasks are graded by mutation kill rate against planted mutants.
ParameterValue
objective_score.verified_task_success0.6
objective_score.hidden_test_score0.15
objective_score.regression_avoidance0.1
objective_score.scope_control0.05
objective_score.cost_efficiency0.05
objective_score.time_efficiency0.05
full_score.objective_score0.95
full_score.blinded_review0.05

Two levels of assessment

Level 1: primary ranking

Who performs best on objective evidence, and which Model-B-over-Model-A gains are material: success delta above threshold and a significant Holm-corrected paired McNemar test. Non-material gains are reported and excluded from escalation.

Level 2: agentic amplification

For material gains only: is the improvement intrinsic capability, or does the newer model simply do more work by default (more tokens, time, tool calls, retries, self-review)? The Agentic Work Index and amplification ratios separate "better" from "busier."

Hardness levels

  • H1 to H2: localized fixes and small multi-step changes.
  • H3: hidden-invariant tasks (e.g. multi-tenant authorization where the naive fix leaks across tenants).
  • H5: state machines and concurrency, e.g. a webhook idempotency race with a deliberately widened window where check-then-act and unlocked guards both fail.

Validity

Runs are quarantined (not counted in ranking) when the served model differs from the requested one (fallback), the baseline suite was broken before the agent started, the run timed out, or the infrastructure crashed (billing, rate limit, provider error). Invalid runs are reported separately with their reason.

Stack & requirements

AgentDelta is a thin, reproducible harness over established, open tools. Nothing about the agent's behavior is simulated: a real coding-agent CLI runs against real repositories in real containers, and every external component is pinned by version or image digest.

What it is built on

ComponentWhat it is, and why AgentDelta uses it
Inspect AIThe UK AI Safety Institute's open-source LLM evaluation framework. It drives each task: provisioning the sandbox, invoking the solver, scoring, and writing the eval log.
inspect_sweAn Inspect AI extension that runs real software-engineering agents as the solver. AgentDelta uses it to run the Claude Code and Codex CLI agents inside the sandbox.
Claude CodeAnthropic's agentic coding CLI (one of the agents under test). It reads files, runs shell commands, edits code, and iterates on test feedback autonomously.
Codex CLIOpenAI's agentic coding CLI (the second agent under test), driven the same way as Claude Code and graded by the same hidden tests, selectable per run with --agent.
Anthropic APIServes the pinned Claude models (opus-4-8 / 4-7 / 4-6 and sonnet-4-6) the Claude Code agent calls.
OpenAI APIServes the pinned GPT-5 models (gpt-5.4 / 5.1 / 5 / 5-mini) the Codex CLI agent calls.
Gemini CLIGoogle's agentic coding CLI, available via inspect_swe and planned as a third provider.
DockerProvides one isolated sandbox container per fixture, pinned by image digest so every run starts from a byte-identical repository state.
pytestRuns the baseline, public, and hidden Python test suites that grade a run.
Node.js test runnerThe built-in node --test runner executes the TypeScript fixture's tests against the compiled output.
TypeScriptOne fixture is a TypeScript library compiled with tsc, giving cross-language coverage.
Gogo test runs the Go fixture's tests; a third language alongside Python and TypeScript.
PythonThe harness language and three of the fixtures (the package toolkit, the multi-tenant service, the payments service, and the long-context ledger).

Agents and providers

AgentDelta runs the same tasks through interchangeable agent CLIs, selected per run with --agent. Each agent talks to its own provider and a pinned model cohort:

  • Claude Code (--agent claude_code) on the Anthropic API: claude-opus-4-8, claude-opus-4-7, claude-opus-4-6, claude-sonnet-4-6.
  • Codex CLI (--agent codex_cli) on the OpenAI API: gpt-5.4, gpt-5.1, gpt-5, gpt-5-mini.
  • Gemini CLI: planned as a third provider (already exposed by inspect_swe).

Cohorts and pinned IDs live in configs/models/; pricing (per provider, with source and date) in agent_delta/scoring/cost.py.

Fixtures and language toolchains

Tasks live in small but realistic repositories ("fixtures"), each built into its own Docker image pinned by digest:

  • Python (4 fixtures) on python:3.12-slim, graded with pytest: a utility toolkit, a layered multi-tenant SaaS service, a payments/webhook service, and a 220-file long-context ledger.
  • TypeScript (1 fixture) on node:20-bookworm-slim, compiled with tsc and graded with the Node.js test runner: a pricing library.
  • Go (1 fixture) on golang:1.22, graded with go test: a text-processing toolkit.

Requirements to reproduce

  • A running Docker daemon (the sandbox images are built and run locally; task verification via agentdelta check-task uses Docker only, no model calls, no cost).
  • A provider API key for real runs: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for Claude Code, OPENAI_API_KEY for Codex CLI. The agent reaches its provider from inside the sandbox.
  • Python 3.12+ in a virtual environment with Inspect AI, inspect_swe, and the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs installed; the chosen agent CLI is provisioned by inspect_swe.
  • Build the per-fixture images once with agentdelta build-sandbox, then agentdelta run-matrix drives the task x model x repetition grid with blocked randomization, and agentdelta report-html renders this document.

Source, fixtures, tasks, and the harness are open at github.com/davidwilliam/agent_delta.

Reproducibility

Each suite carries a manifest: tool versions, host, agent CLI version, content hashes of tasks/scoring/fixtures/hidden-tests, sandbox image digests, and the seeded run order. Drift in any hash is detectable with agentdelta validate-reproducibility.

About AgentDelta

AgentDelta measures the delta between coding-agent systems with objective, reproducible evidence, and refuses to report a difference it cannot defend statistically.

What it is

A benchmark that evaluates a model-plus-agent system end to end. Each task is a real repository with a planted bug or a missing feature; a coding agent (Claude Code on Anthropic or Codex CLI on OpenAI) works autonomously inside a pinned Docker sandbox, and the result is graded by hidden tests the agent never sees, alongside a regression suite and an edit-scope check. The same tasks run across providers, so agents are compared on a level field. Every run records the full resource footprint: tokens, cost, wall-clock time, tool calls, retries, and diff size.

Scoring is two-level. Level 1 ranks systems on objective success and asks which gains are material (a meaningful success delta that also survives a Holm-corrected paired McNemar test). Level 2, the Agentic Amplification Assessment, takes only the material gains and asks whether a newer model is genuinely better or merely does more work by default, by comparing it under normalized conditions (equal budget, matched workflow, strong spec).

Why it exists

Coding-agent capability is usually communicated through demos and single-number leaderboards. Those answer "can the model produce a plausible answer?" AgentDelta is built to answer a harder, more useful question:

Can the model make the correct change, in the correct place, with the correct scope, preserving hidden invariants, passing hidden tests, avoiding shortcuts, and doing so at an acceptable cost in time, tokens, and money?

Four convictions shape the design:

  • Objective over impressionistic. A beautiful patch that fails a hidden edge case, weakens a test, or leaks across tenants should fail. Grading is by tests and diffs, not taste.
  • Capability is not the same as more work. A model that wins only by spending 5x the tokens and 4x the tool calls is amplified, not necessarily more capable. Separating the two is the whole point of the Level 2 assessment, and it changes what you should pay for.
  • "No difference" is a real, valuable result. When models are statistically tied, the benchmark says so rather than manufacturing a ranking from noise. The materiality gate exists to earn the right to make, or withhold, a claim.
  • Reproducibility is non-negotiable. Pinned models, pinned images by digest, content-hashed tasks and tests, seeded run order. A result you cannot reproduce is an anecdote.

The practical payoff is an honest, cost-and-latency-aware comparison: not just "which model is best" but "which is best for a weak-spec user, a budget-constrained user, or a long-horizon task," and whether paying for a newer model buys capability or just buys more tokens.

How to read this report

  • Results leads with the headline and the honest interpretation.
  • Per-model and Per-suite hold the detailed tables.
  • Statistics shows the materiality gates (McNemar / Holm) behind every claim.
  • Raw runs is the ground truth: every run, every metric.
  • Methodology and Stack & requirements document how it works and what it runs on; Reproducibility carries the manifests.

Source

AgentDelta is open source at github.com/davidwilliam/agent_delta. The repository contains the harness, all fixtures, the task suite, the scoring subsystem, and the report generator that produced this page.
